short_17920726.summary: Short's private complaint at being passed over for Paris in favour of Gouverneur Morris: Lafayette's mortification, the French diplomatic committee's wish to refuse Morris, and Short's preferences for a post (the Hague as resident, Spain as plenipotentiary) and for the grades of the American diplomatic establishment.
short_17920726.en:
(f. 0160999) ... the class of people called les intriguants ...

(f. 0161001) I mentioned to you in a former letter how much the Mar fai had been and mortified at this circumstance.

(ff. 0161005-1009) You there are so good as to state to me the precarious footing on which I stand and to desire me to do in this what I chuse, informing you of my wishes that you may cooperate with them. Encouraged by this kind and friendly offer I resume a subject which I had so much repented having formerly importuned you about, namely my wishes as to my own personal advancement. My reasons for not desiring to return to America as yet, and with which you are acquainted, and my being thus launched in the diplomatic career, put me absolutely in the power of government, so that they may do what they please; for the present I am obliged to accept and obey.

carmichael_17880414.summary: A clear letter with five code numbers used as a test of his cypher: Maryland (twice), Massachusetts and the majority on the ratification of the Constitution; the last item (597) stays open. The read share of 0% counts only the five code groups: none has a value attested in another letter (four are context conjectures, 597 is open), and the clear text of the letter is not counted.
carmichael_17880414.en:
Had I been in [Maryland] I should in all probability have been of the sentiment of Paca and the other you mention.
[Maryland] has not acceded to the Constitution, [Massachusetts] has. The [majority] seem pleased with it, what says 597?

pinckney_17930828.summary: Three coded sentences: regiments are to embark shortly on a secret expedition under Sir Charles Grey with Generals Stuart and a second general whose name is not recovered (the editors conjectured Dundas), generally thought to be for the West Indies; the number of regiments (447) stays open.
pinckney_17930828.en: 447 regiments are to embark in a short time on a secret expedition. They are to be commanded by Sir Charles Grey with Generals Stuart and [?55]ats under him. Their destination is generally thought to be for the West Indies.

pinckney_179508.summary: The coded phrases of Pinckney's letters from Spain during his negotiation of the treaty of 1795, sent again in the Department's cipher ("Cypher 2d") with a covering letter of 27 August: Spain's wish for delay, a triple alliance with France, and a guarantee of her American possessions. The enclosure holds only the coded passages, so each stands apart from its clear sentence.
pinckney_179508.en:
The cyphered part of the letter of 21 July 1795 (frame 0019 left, then 0018):

That they are still anxious for further delay, which is to them equivalent to a cession of our rights so long as we shall acquiesce therein, they being in possession of the object of controversy.
not guarantee the possessions of Spain in America.
Stipulations on this subject in our treaty with france should be observed.
Their accomodation with france.
Establish a triple alliance between france, Spain and ourselves.
an alliance.
Intentions of the french government with respect to our negotiation here.
French commissioners have complied with their instructions.
[...] minister at paris offered an accommodation between Spain and france unless our rights were previously acknowledged by the former.
This court means to proceed in their system of delay, or whether they will yield to us our rights.

pinckney_179510.summary: Coded stretches from Pinckney's letter of 28 October 1795 with his notes on the treaty, and of 18 December from Paris: he had asked for his passports when an accommodation seemed impossible; Spain wished to keep her commercial advantages as the equivalent for a guarantee of her American possessions. Only the coded lines were transcribed, and the binding hides line ends, so the text is fragments.
pinckney_179510.en:
San Lorenzo, 28 October 1795 (frame 0111):

[...] note of the twenty fourth of October that I found the [?difficulties] of such an accommodation as I could accede to were so insuperable that I had asked for my passports to return. This may illustrate the difficulties I had to encounter and the prejudices to be removed, which requires some knowledge of the national character fully to conceive. The peace concluded between this Country and France and the [?prominent] disposition (at least exteriorly) exhibited to Spain by the british cabinet, added to our critical situation with the last power, [...] rendered this negotiation [...]
[...] besides which I believe they wish to reserve the commercial advantages they can offer as the equivalent [?for] a guarantee of their american possessions.

eaton_18010525.summary: Eaton reports Tripoli's declaration of war and proposes, in code, to seize the Tripolitan commodore Morad Rais (the renegade Peter Lisle) by approaching corsairs under English colours, and to go on board the American squadron himself, leaving Cathcart in charge at Tunis.
eaton_18010525.en:
On the eleventh instant War was declared in form by the Bashaw of Tripoli against the United States of America. A few days before this event took place the Commodore's Ship was dressed with the flags of all Nations: that of the United States was hoisted forward, in the place of prize flags, under the Neapolitan.

This Commodore [?is] a British Renegade, Morad Rais; Alias, Peter Lisle. We must get possession of him. For this purpose let our ships of war approach all [?Barbary] corsaires under English colours till they are distinguishable. They all wear the same flag. Lisle once secured, a stratagem may be used to decoy the [?Bashaw] into an American frigate and thus end the war.

Mr. Cathcart is expected here in a few days. Persuaded that I could be more serviceable to the squadron than here at this crisis, I take liberty to propose leaving Mr.

eaton_18021009.summary: The Bey thanks the President for the stores and jewels sent under the treaty and asks for a frigate of thirty-six guns. Eaton's own postscript, in the same code, proposes taking Porto Farina by surprise and destroying the Bey's arsenal and ships if the letter provokes resentment.

eaton_18021022.summary: Eaton repeats in code, in a recapitulating letter, his proposal of 9 October to take Porto Farina and destroy the Bey's naval arsenal.
eaton_18021022.en:
... Its stile is indicative of a resolution in the author not to receive a negative.

If the [?letter] should provoke resentment, Porto Farina may be taken by surprise or stratagem with 800 men, and the Bey's whole naval arsenal, together with his [?large] vessels of war, destroyed. But it would require [?secrecy] and [?address]. It would be a [?vital] wound to [?cruising]. But it should be done in the winter or spring season.

lear_181301.summary: Lear reports that on 31 December the Spanish Regency laid before the Cortes an exposition of American conduct toward Spain (East Florida, agents in the Spanish colonies, the forces near Baton Rouge, Onis's correspondence) and would recommend war if Spain's circumstances allowed; it was referred in secret session to a commission. The sheet arrived under a blank cover and was read at the Department with 'Mr Lears Cypher'.
lear_181301.en: 31st December the Regency of this Kingdom presented to the Cortes General and Extraordinary what they term an exposition of the conduct of the United States toward Spain before the revolution in Spain to the present time. This paper enters generally into the conduct adopted by the Agent of the United States resident here, the possession of East Florida, the numerous incendiaries employed by the Executive of the United States in different parts of their american possessions, naming several, particularly a doctor Robinson; the forces collecting near baton rouge, as intended to join the insurgents in Mexico: but more particularly the correspondence of the Chavalier Onis, which exhibits many unfounded speculations and false conclusions upon subjects that he is totally unacquainted with, or which he has viewed thro a false medium.
